# Setting Up Your Workstation {#sec-workstation} A workstation is the one piece of infrastructure in this book that nobody will ever ask you about. No reviewer inspects it, no funder requires it, and no collaborator sees it, so it tends to stay in whatever state it arrived in. Its defects do not announce themselves. They appear as friction: a path that works here and not there, a package that is a different version than you thought, a script that runs in your session only because yesterday's objects were quietly restored into it. This chapter installs the minimum a professional biostatistician needs (R, an editor, Quarto, and Git), on macOS, Windows, or Linux, and ends with a checklist that tells you in four commands whether your machine is ready for the rest of the book. ::: {.bookepigraph} ```{=latex} \begin{flushright}\small ``` *Man is a Tool-using Animal. ... Nowhere do you find him without Tools; without Tools he is nothing, with Tools he is all.* [Thomas Carlyle]{.smallcaps}, *Sartor Resartus* (1833--34) ```{=latex} \end{flushright} ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Where this chapter sits: the workstation is the Environment band at its most basic, the tools every stage of the analysis runs on.](04-workstation_files/figure-html/fig-workstation-pipeline-1.png){#fig-workstation-pipeline fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). Highlighted for this chapter: Environment.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title='In this chapter'} **Reading time.** About 20 minutes, plus an hour or so of installing. **You'll need.** @sec-shell for the terminal, and permission to install software on your machine. The chapter loads no packages; the checklist at its end installs `renv` with `install.packages("renv")`. **You'll be able to.** - Install R, an IDE (integrated development environment), Quarto, and Git on macOS, Windows (natively or under WSL), or Linux, choosing one route for each. - Predict where `install.packages()` puts a package, with and without a project library. - Keep the user-level `.Rprofile` minimal, stop workspace restoration, and keep secrets out of code. - Verify a machine with the 'Is my machine ready?' checklist. **Outline.** - [The essentials](#sec-workstation-essentials) - [Installing, by operating system](#sec-workstation-install) - [Where R finds packages](#sec-workstation-libpaths) - [Startup files and secrets](#sec-workstation-rprofile) - [Is my machine ready?](#sec-workstation-ready) - [Level up (optional)](#sec-workstation-levelup) ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Skip ahead?'} If these answers come quickly, skip to the next chapter. The answers are in @sec-quiz-answers-04. 1. When you install a new R package on your workstation, where does R store it by default, and how would you check that location? 2. What does a restored `.RData` workspace do to a script that you believe runs from a clean start? 3. Which commands tell you whether R, Quarto, Git, and a project's packages are ready to use? ::: ## The essentials {#sec-workstation-essentials} The goal is not a comfortable machine; comfort is a matter of taste this book has no standing to legislate. The goal is a legible one: a configuration that is written down, restorable, and separable from the projects that run on it, so that the analysis you run on Tuesday gives the same result on Wednesday, and the one you run at home gives the same result as in the office. @tbl-workstation-essentials is the whole of what the rest of the book assumes. | Tool | What it is for | Taught in | |---|---|---| | R, version 4.4 or later | Every analysis in the book | Throughout | | An IDE: RStudio, Positron, or VS Code | Writing and running R and Quarto | This chapter | | Quarto | Rendering documents that compute their own numbers | @sec-quarto | | Git, with a GitHub account | Version control and sharing | @sec-git-solo | | `renv` (an R package) | Pinning a project's package versions | @sec-renv | : The essentials path. Everything else in this chapter is optional. {#tbl-workstation-essentials} Two judgments matter more than any choice of product. First, **pin the foundational toolchain.** Know which version of R and Quarto you run, change it deliberately, and record it per project; casual updates are how reproducibility breaks silently. `rig`, the R installation manager, keeps several R versions side by side on macOS, Windows, and Linux, and Docker (@sec-docker) pins the rest. Second, **install each tool by one route.** Two installers for the same tool compete for the same directories, and which copy runs then depends on the order of your `PATH`. ### Choosing an IDE Take the conclusion first: the choice matters much less than the fluency. The productivity you gain by knowing one editor thoroughly exceeds anything available by switching to a better one, and a year spent shallowly in three of them is worse than a year spent deeply in any one. What the choice does turn on is fit, along two axes: whether your work is R-only or spans several languages, and whether it happens on your own machine or on a server you reach over SSH (Secure Shell). | IDE | What it is | Choose it when | |---|---|---| | RStudio | Posit's IDE for R: editor, console, environment, plots, help, and a Git pane in one window | R is your main language; you want zero setup; you teach or collaborate with RStudio users | | Positron | Posit's newer IDE for R and Python, built on the same open-source base as VS Code[^positron] | You work in both R and Python and want an R-aware IDE | | VS Code | A general editor with an R extension and strong remote editing (SSH, WSL, containers) | You work in several languages, or edit on a remote server or inside WSL | : Three IDEs for R. All are used professionally in biostatistics. {#tbl-workstation-ides} [^positron]: As of 2026-10, Positron has stable releases, with some components still labeled experimental. RStudio remains the dominant choice in academic biostatistics, and VS Code the fastest-growing alternative. Keyboard-driven editors such as Neovim are a fourth option for people who already use them; @sec-workstation-levelup has the details. ### Exercises 1. Install the tools in @tbl-workstation-essentials, then record the version of each with `R --version`, `quarto --version`, and `git --version`. In your IDE's R console, run `R.version.string`. Does it match the terminal's `R --version`? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} They should match. If the IDE reports a different R from the terminal, two R installations are present and the IDE and the terminal find different ones first; that is the competing-routes problem above. In RStudio, Tools > Global Options > General shows which R it uses (on Windows it can be changed there); with `rig`, `rig list` shows every installed version and `rig default` sets the one both find. Remove the installation you did not mean to have rather than living with two. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A colleague installed R from the installer on CRAN (the Comprehensive R Archive Network) a year ago and later ran `brew install r` to get a newer version. What can go wrong? **Answer.** Two R installations now exist, each with its own library of packages. Which one starts depends on the order of the `PATH` (for the terminal) and on the IDE's settings, which need not agree. A package installed from the terminal may then be missing in the IDE, or a script may run under a different R version than the one recorded in the project's lockfile. Keep one route per tool, and use `rig` when you genuinely need several versions. ::: ## Installing, by operating system {#sec-workstation-install} Install in the order of the tabs' steps: Git first (on macOS and Windows it brings tools that later steps use), then R, then the IDE and Quarto. Download links change; the pages named below are the stable entry points as of 2026-10. ::: {.panel-tabset} ### macOS 1. **Command-line tools and Git.** `xcode-select --install` installs Apple's compilers and Git. 2. **R**, by one of two routes: ```bash # either: a single system R from the CRAN installer brew install --cask r # or (better, and instead of the above): rig manages # multiple R versions brew tap r-lib/rig brew install --cask rig rig install release # latest stable rig install 4.4.0 # specific version rig default 4.4.0 ``` Choose one of the two routes, not both; installing R through the cask and again through `rig` leaves two installers competing for the same framework directory. Both use Homebrew (`brew.sh`); without it, the CRAN installer from `cran.r-project.org` is the first route. 3. **The IDE and Quarto.** `brew install --cask rstudio quarto`, or the installers from `posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/`, `positron.posit.co`, and `quarto.org/docs/get-started/`. On Apple Silicon, use the `arm64` build of R; Homebrew lives in `/opt/homebrew`, not `/usr/local`. ### Windows 1. **Git for Windows** from `git-scm.com/download/win`. It also installs Git Bash, the `bash` terminal that @sec-shell uses. Its installer asks how to treat line endings; the default (check out Windows-style, commit Unix-style) is right, and @sec-git-teams shows how a repository makes the rule explicit. 2. **R** from `cran.r-project.org` (Download R for Windows, then 'base'), or `rig` from its releases page, which also manages versions. Install **Rtools** as well, whose version must match R's minor version (Rtools44 for R 4.4); it is needed whenever a package has to be compiled from source. 3. **The IDE and Quarto** from the installers at `posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/` (or Positron or VS Code) and `quarto.org/docs/get-started/`. R on Windows accepts forward slashes in paths (`"C:/Users/you/project"`); a backslash must be doubled (`"C:\\Users\\you\\project"`) because it is R's escape character. ### Windows with WSL WSL (the Windows Subsystem for Linux) runs a real Linux system inside Windows, so that the commands in this book, the Docker images of @sec-docker, and the servers you will later use all behave the same way. In an administrator PowerShell: ```bash wsl --install ``` This installs WSL 2 with Ubuntu as the default distribution. Open Ubuntu from the Start menu, create a user, and follow the **Linux** tab inside it. Two rules make WSL pleasant: - Keep projects in the Linux filesystem (under `~/` inside Ubuntu), not under `/mnt/c/`. File access across the boundary is much slower, and Windows tools may rewrite line endings. - Edit with an IDE that can reach inside WSL. VS Code with its WSL extension runs the editor in Windows and R in Linux. RStudio Desktop for Windows uses a Windows installation of R, not the R inside WSL. ### Linux On Ubuntu or Debian: ```bash sudo apt update sudo apt install --no-install-recommends r-base r-base-dev git ``` The distribution's R can lag the current release; for the latest version, add the CRAN apt repository (see `cran.r-project.org/bin/linux/ubuntu/`), or use `rig`, which also runs on Linux. Packages from CRAN are compiled from source on Linux by default, which is slow and needs system libraries; Posit Public Package Manager serves prebuilt Linux binaries, and its setup page gives the repository URL for your distribution.[^p3m-04] Install the IDE and Quarto from their `.deb` packages, for example `sudo apt install ./quarto--linux-amd64.deb`. ::: [^p3m-04]: The same service serves CRAN as it stood on a given date, which @sec-renv uses to make restores reproducible. ### After installing: Git and Quarto Tell Git who you are, once per machine (the name and email appear in every commit you make): ```bash git config --global user.name "Your Name" git config --global user.email "you@example.com" git config --global core.editor "code --wait" # or your editor git config --global init.defaultBranch main ``` For Quarto, check the version, and pin it per project if a document depends on it: ```bash # verify version quarto --version # in a project's _quarto.yml, optionally require a # version range (rendering stops with an error otherwise) # quarto-required: ">= 1.5.55" ``` The `quarto-required` key does not install anything; it makes a render on the wrong version fail loudly instead of succeeding quietly with different output. ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} A model can draft a bootstrap script for a new machine; the check is the checklist in @sec-workstation-ready, not the model's assurance. > **Context.** I am setting up [macOS 15 on Apple Silicon | Windows > 11 with WSL 2 and Ubuntu 24.04 | Ubuntu 24.04]. I need R > (through `rig`), [RStudio | Positron | VS Code], Quarto, and Git, > configured with my name and email. > > **Constraints.** Install each tool by exactly one route. Do not > use `sudo` except for the system package manager. Do not pipe a > downloaded script into a shell except for an installer whose > documentation prescribes it, and name that documentation. Make > the script safe to run twice. > > **Criteria.** The script ends by running `R --version`, > `quarto check`, and `git config --list`, and the last line it > prints says which of them failed, if any. *Failure mode.* The model writes for the wrong platform (an Ubuntu script when you said macOS), assumes Intel paths (`/usr/local` rather than `/opt/homebrew` on Apple Silicon), or installs R twice by two routes. *Check.* Run it in a fresh virtual machine or a new user account, then run every row of @tbl-workstation-ready yourself. The prompt contains no data, only your platform. ::: ### Exercises 2. Install `rig` and use it to install two R versions side by side (for example the current release and 4.4). Install a small package in each. How can you show that the two versions keep separate user libraries? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} Start each version (`rig default `, then `R`) and run `.libPaths()[1]`: the user library's path ends in the R minor version, for example `.../4.4/library` on macOS or `~/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/4.4` on Linux. After `install.packages("praise")` in one version, `find.package("praise")` succeeds there and fails with 'there is no package called' in the other. Packages are built for one minor version of R, which is why each keeps its own library. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** On Windows with WSL, you keep your project under `/mnt/c/Users/you/project` so that you can open it from Windows too. What does that cost? **Answer.** Speed and, potentially, line endings. Every file operation crosses from Linux to the Windows filesystem, which is much slower for the many small files a project with a package library contains, and Windows editors that touch the files may write CRLF endings that the Linux tools then read (@sec-shell shows what a stray carriage return does to a count). Keep the project in `~/` inside WSL and edit it with an IDE that reaches into WSL. ::: ## Where R finds packages {#sec-workstation-libpaths} Almost every 'it works on my machine' report about a missing or wrong-version package resolves to one question: which library did R look in? @fig-libpaths is the search order, and the thing to notice is that `renv` works by replacing the user and site libraries rather than by adding to them. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-libpaths %%| fig-alt: "Decision flowchart starting from a library(dplyr) %%| call. If an active project renv library is present, the %%| project-pinned version is used. If not, the user library is %%| searched, then the site and system libraries. All three %%| outcomes converge on a node reading 'first match wins'." %%| fig-cap: "The library search path. R takes the first match it %%| finds, and installs into the first entry. Activating `renv` %%| puts the project library first and removes the user and site %%| libraries, which is why the same `install.packages()` call %%| lands in different places depending on where you ran it." flowchart TD Q["library(dplyr)"] --> A{"project renv library
present and active?"} A -->|"yes"| B["renv/library/...
project-pinned version"] A -->|"no"| C{"user library"} C -->|"found"| D["~/Library/R/...
whatever you last installed"] C -->|"not found"| E["site and system libraries
whatever the admin installed"] B --> F["first match wins"] D --> F E --> F ``` R looks for packages in the directories returned by `.libPaths()` (display-only, because the paths are machine-specific): ```r .libPaths() #> [1] "/Users/you/Library/R/arm64/4.4/library" #> [2] "/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/4.4-arm64/Resources/library" ``` The first is your user library; later entries are system libraries. `install.packages()` installs into `.libPaths()[1]` by default. The paths shown are for the CRAN build of R 4.4 on an Apple Silicon Mac; yours will differ by platform, R version, and installer (a Homebrew-built R, for example, reports directories under `/opt/homebrew/`), so run the call rather than trust the listing. With `renv` active in a project, the project's `renv/library/` takes precedence: ```r .libPaths() #> [1] "/path/to/project/renv/library/macos/R-4.4/aarch64-apple-darwin20" #> [2] "/Users/you/Library/Caches/org.R-project.R/R/renv/sandbox/..." ``` Your user library is no longer on the list at all; the second entry is a sandboxed view of the system library. This is what `renv` does: each project has its own package library, isolated from other projects and from your user library (@sec-renv covers `renv` in depth). The pattern that follows: - The user library holds a small set of packages used across projects (`usethis`, `devtools`, `rmarkdown`, perhaps `tidyverse`), updated when convenient. - Project libraries, under `renv`, hold the version-pinned dependencies of each analysis. ### Exercises 3. In an R session outside any project, run `.libPaths()[1]`, install a package, and confirm with `find.package()` where it went. Then open a project that uses `renv` and repeat. What changed, and what did `renv.lock` record? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} Outside the project, `find.package("")` returns a path under your user library, the first entry of `.libPaths()`. Inside the `renv` project, the first entry is the project library, and the package lands there; your user library does not change. `renv.lock` records nothing until you run `renv::snapshot()`, and `renv::status()` meanwhile reports the package as installed but not recorded once the project's code uses it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** You run `install.packages("dplyr")` from inside a project that has `renv` active. Where does it install, and does the lockfile change? **Answer.** Into the project's `renv/library/` directory, not the user library. `renv` modifies `.libPaths()` so that the first entry is the project library, and `install.packages()` installs to the first entry. The lock file (`renv.lock`) is *not* updated: it changes only when you run `renv::snapshot()`, and until then `renv::status()` flags the package as installed but not recorded once the project's code uses it. This isolation is the point of `renv`: a package update inside one project does not affect any other project's packages. ::: ## Startup files and secrets {#sec-workstation-rprofile} Anything in a user-level `.Rprofile` runs at the start of every session and changes its behavior. A heavy one (loading `tidyverse`, setting global options, defining helpers) makes your sessions different from a colleague's, and lets a script that does not load what it needs run on your machine and fail on theirs. Keep the user-level file nearly empty; a project-level `.Rprofile` is part of the project and runs for anyone who opens it. Things that *are* fine in `~/.Rprofile`: ```r # ~/.Rprofile # friendlier defaults options( repos = c(CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org/"), prompt = "R> ", continue = " + ", digits = 7, warnPartialMatchArgs = TRUE, warnPartialMatchAttr = TRUE, warnPartialMatchDollar = TRUE ) # only attach interactively (not in scripts or knitting) if (interactive()) { suppressMessages(require(devtools)) } ``` Things to avoid in it: | Avoid | Because | |---|---| | `library(tidyverse)` | Scripts come to depend on it silently | | Defining helper functions | Collaborators do not have them | | `options(stringsAsFactors = FALSE)` | Harmless since R 4.0, and a sign of muscle memory from older versions | : What stays out of the user-level `.Rprofile`. {#tbl-workstation-rprofile} `renv` itself uses a project `.Rprofile` to activate the project library. Anything else in a project `.Rprofile` should be deliberate, because every collaborator runs it. ### The restored workspace R can save every object in a session to a file named `.RData` when it quits, and restore them when it next starts in that directory. RStudio offers to do both by default. The chunk below makes the consequence concrete: it saves a `cohort` object into an `.RData` file in a temporary directory, then starts R there twice, once as an IDE does and once with `--vanilla`, which skips the restore. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} proj <- file.path(tempdir(), "restore-demo") dir.create(proj, showWarnings = FALSE) cohort <- data.frame(id = 1:3) save(cohort, file = file.path(proj, ".RData")) r_bin <- file.path(R.home("bin"), "R") start_r <- function(flags) { old <- setwd(proj) on.exit(setwd(old)) writeLines(system2(r_bin, c(flags, "--no-echo", "-e", shQuote("exists('cohort')")), stdout = TRUE)) } start_r(c("--no-save", "--no-init-file")) #> [1] TRUE start_r("--vanilla") #> [1] FALSE unlink(proj, recursive = TRUE) ``` ::: The first session finds `cohort` although no code in it created the object; the second, a clean start, does not. (The first also skips your `.Rprofile`, so that the workspace is the only difference.) ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **A restored workspace makes a broken script run.** If a script uses an object it never creates, because you deleted the line that built it or built it by hand in the console last week, the restored `.RData` supplies it and the script runs, on stale data, in your session only. A collaborator, a fresh clone, or a render fails, or worse, runs on a different object of the same name. Turn the restore off once: `usethis::use_blank_slate()` sets RStudio never to save or restore the workspace (in Tools > Global Options > General), and running `R --vanilla`, or Session > Restart R before a final run, gives a clean start. ::: ### Secrets stay out of code Passwords, API (application programming interface) keys, and tokens belong in neither a script nor a startup file that might be shared. Two places are standard: ```r # ~/.Renviron (user-level; never in a repository) # REDCAP_TOKEN=paste-the-token-here Sys.getenv("REDCAP_TOKEN") # or the operating system's credential store keyring::key_set("redcap") # prompts; stores in the keychain keyring::key_get("redcap") ``` `~/.Renviron` is read at startup and its variables are available through `Sys.getenv()`; it lives in your home directory, outside every project, and a project-level `.Renviron` must be listed in `.gitignore` (@sec-git-solo). The `keyring` package stores the secret in the macOS Keychain, the Windows Credential Manager, or the Linux Secret Service, so that it is never in a plain-text file at all (display-only: both change your machine's state). ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} When R fails at startup or behaves differently in your IDE than in a terminal, a model can narrow the cause if you give it the startup evidence. > **Context.** Below are the error or unexpected behavior, the > output of `sessionInfo()`, `.libPaths()`, and > `Sys.getenv(c("R_LIBS_USER", "R_PROFILE_USER"))`, and the > contents of my `~/.Rprofile` and the project's `.Rprofile`, with > every token and password replaced by ``. > > **Constraints.** Do not suggest reinstalling R or deleting the > library. Propose diagnostics before fixes, one at a time. > > **Criteria.** Name the most likely cause among: a startup file > doing something unexpected, a restored `.RData` workspace, a > second R installation or library on the path, and an inactive > `renv` project. Give the command that would confirm it. *Failure mode.* A generic answer ('reinstall the package') that treats the symptom, or a diagnosis that ignores the workspace: a restored `.RData` is a common cause of 'works in my session only', and models rarely raise it unprompted. *Check.* Run R with `--vanilla`, which skips both startup files and the restore; if the problem disappears, add them back one at a time. Startup files can contain secrets, so redact before sending, and send no data (@sec-ai-governance). ::: ### Exercises 4. Compare your `~/.Rprofile` (if you have one) with @tbl-workstation-rprofile, and run `usethis::use_blank_slate()`. Then, in a temporary directory, reproduce the restore demonstration above with your own R: what do the two sessions print? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} The output of the demonstration chunk above is the key: the session that restores the workspace prints `TRUE`, and the `--vanilla` session prints `FALSE`. Anything in your `.Rprofile` that loads packages, defines functions, or sets options that change results (`digits` aside) belongs in the project that needs it, written as code the project runs. `usethis::use_blank_slate()` reports that it set the two workspace options; check them in RStudio's General options. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** You moved a database password from a script into `.Renviron` in the project directory. Is it now safe? **Answer.** Only if the project's `.gitignore` lists `.Renviron` and the file was never committed. A project-level `.Renviron` sits in the repository's working tree, so `git add .` stages it like any other file, and a password in any earlier commit is exposed for good (@sec-git-solo). The user-level `~/.Renviron`, outside every project, or the system keychain through `keyring`, avoids the question. ::: ## Is my machine ready? {#sec-workstation-ready} Run the four checks in @tbl-workstation-ready from a terminal. Later chapters point back here when they assume a working setup. | Check | Command | Ready when | |---|---|---| | R is installed and found | `R --version` | Prints R 4.4 or later, the version you meant to install | | Quarto finds its tools and R | `quarto check` | Every section ends in `OK`, and the R section lists `knitr` and `rmarkdown` | | Git knows who you are | `git config --list` | The list includes `user.name`, `user.email`, and `init.defaultBranch=main` | | A project's packages match its lockfile | `Rscript -e 'renv::status()'`, run in a project that uses `renv` | It reports no issues | : The 'Is my machine ready?' checklist. {#tbl-workstation-ready} The last row needs a project; the book's own repository, or the practice repository of @sec-git-solo once you have initialized `renv` in it, will do. `install.packages("renv")` installs the package into your user library first. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Run the checklist on a machine you did not set up yourself (a lab computer, a colleague's laptop, or a fresh user account on yours). A check that passes only on your own account depends on something in your home directory, most often a startup file or an `.RData` workspace. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** `quarto check` reports `OK` for everything except the R section, which says it cannot find R, although `R --version` works in the same terminal. What is the likely cause? **Answer.** Quarto looks for R through the `PATH` and, on some systems, through `QUARTO_R`; a second installation, or an R the IDE knows about but the `PATH` does not, produces exactly this split. Run `which R` (or `where R` on Windows) to see which executable the terminal finds. If you use `rig`, `rig default` makes one version the one both find; otherwise, set `QUARTO_R` to the R you mean. ::: ## Level up (optional) {#sec-workstation-levelup} Nothing in this section is needed for the rest of the book. It collects the configuration that experienced analysts add once the essentials are routine: a keyboard-driven editor, a shell that remembers more, readable fonts, and a way to rebuild all of it on a new machine. ### Editors beyond the IDE Neovim, with an R plugin, is the keyboard-driven modal editor: highly customizable, fast, and usable over SSH without modification, with a steep learning curve. The capability that makes it viable for analysis rather than merely for editing is a link to a live R session: `R.nvim` is the established choice, and the in-house `zzvim-R` is the lighter one used in this book's own development, sending the current line, a visual selection, or a whole Quarto chunk to an embedded terminal. Its render command calls `rmarkdown::render()` rather than `quarto render`, so a `@fig-` cross-reference stays as literal text in the output; render from the terminal, or with a dedicated Quarto editor integration, when cross-references matter. Choose it if you already use vi or Neovim for other languages, or do most of your work over SSH. ### Shell and terminal On macOS and most Linux systems `zsh` is the default interactive shell. A minimal `~/.zshrc`: ```bash # minimal zshrc # history HISTFILE=~/.zsh_history HISTSIZE=10000 SAVEHIST=10000 setopt SHARE_HISTORY HIST_IGNORE_DUPS # prompt: starship is a good default eval "$(starship init zsh)" # R-friendly aliases alias R='R --no-save' alias r='R --quiet --no-save' # editor export EDITOR='code' # brew completions on macOS (zsh, not bash, completion) if type brew &>/dev/null; then FPATH="$(brew --prefix)/share/zsh/site-functions:${FPATH}" autoload -Uz compinit compinit fi ``` `starship` (`starship.rs`, `brew install starship`) gives a fast prompt that shows the Git branch. `tmux` is worth learning if you work on servers over SSH: its sessions survive disconnection, with several panes and named windows. A minimal `.tmux.conf`: ``` set -g default-terminal "screen-256color" set -g mouse on set -g status-position top bind-key C-a send-prefix unbind C-b set -g prefix C-a ``` For local work you do not need `tmux`; the IDE's session management suffices. ### Fonts Programming fonts distinguish similar characters (0 and O; 1, l, and I), and some render `>=` as a single glyph (a ligature). JetBrains Mono (`jetbrains.com/lp/mono`) and Fira Code have ligatures; Adobe's Source Code Pro does not. Nerd Fonts patch common programming fonts with the extra glyphs that prompts such as `starship` use: ```bash brew install --cask font-jetbrains-mono-nerd-font ``` Set the font in your terminal and editor; in RStudio, under Tools > Global Options > Appearance. ### Dotfiles in version control Your `.zshrc`, `.gitconfig`, `.Rprofile`, `init.vim` (Neovim), and editor settings are configuration you will want on every machine you use. Version-controlling them prevents 'I forgot what I changed last time'. A common layout: ``` ~/dotfiles/ ├── zsh/ │ ├── .zshrc │ └── .zsh_aliases ├── git/ │ └── .gitconfig ├── R/ │ └── .Rprofile ├── nvim/ │ └── init.vim ├── README.md └── install.sh # symlinks files into place ``` GNU `stow` (or `chezmoi`, or `yadm`) symlinks the files into place: ```bash cd ~/dotfiles stow zsh git R nvim # symlinks ~/.zshrc -> ~/dotfiles/zsh/.zshrc, etc. ``` Push the dotfiles repository to GitHub as a *private* repository. Shell histories, `.gitconfig` email addresses, internal hostnames, and the occasional token pasted into `.zshrc` all end up in dotfiles; make the repository public only after you have audited every file for them. Keep secrets out of it entirely, in `~/.Renviron` or the keychain (@sec-workstation-rprofile). On a new machine: ```bash git clone https://github.com/you/dotfiles.git ~/dotfiles cd ~/dotfiles stow zsh git R nvim ``` ### A fresh-laptop script The steps of this chapter, for macOS, as one script (display-only: it changes a machine): ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash # fresh-mac.sh: bootstrap a new macOS workstation # Homebrew /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)" eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)" # core tools brew install git tmux starship stow brew install --cask font-jetbrains-mono rstudio quarto # R via rig only, so that R is not installed twice brew tap r-lib/rig brew install --cask rig rig install release # clone and apply dotfiles git clone https://github.com/you/dotfiles.git ~/dotfiles cd ~/dotfiles && stow zsh git R nvim # install commonly-used global R packages Rscript -e 'install.packages(c("renv", "usethis", "devtools", "remotes", "rmarkdown"))' echo "Setup complete. Reboot recommended." ``` The first command downloads a script and pipes it straight into `bash`, which runs whatever the server returns with your privileges. That is the installation method Homebrew documents, and it is acceptable for a source you have decided to trust, over HTTPS (an encrypted, authenticated connection); it is not a pattern to copy for an arbitrary URL. When in doubt, download the script, read it, and then run it. The `brew shellenv` line is needed on Apple Silicon, where Homebrew lives in `/opt/homebrew` and is not yet on the `PATH` of the shell running the script. Refine the script each time you set up a new machine, and end it with the checklist in @tbl-workstation-ready. ## Rules of thumb 1. **Habit 4: pin the environment.** One installation route per tool, versions you can name, and `quarto-required` or a lockfile wherever a result depends on a version. 2. **Habit 1: the compendium is the unit.** Nothing an analysis needs may live only in your `.Rprofile`, your workspace, or your memory; start clean and let the project load what it uses. 3. **Habit 8: a bug that produces a plausible number is the expensive kind.** A restored workspace turns a broken script into a working one with stale data; turn the restore off. ## Cumulative practice 5. *Cumulative (uses @sec-shell).* Write `check-machine.sh`, a script that runs the four checks in @tbl-workstation-ready and exits with a non-zero status if any fails. Run it on your machine, then make one check fail on purpose (for example by running it with `PATH` stripped of Quarto) and confirm that the script says so. 6. *On your own work (no key).* For a completed analysis of your own, find three hard-coded paths or other machine-specific assumptions and refactor them away, then run the analysis from a fresh clone with `R --vanilla`. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} One version, which reports every check before deciding: ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash # check-machine.sh: the 'Is my machine ready?' checklist set -uo pipefail failed=0 check() { if "$@" > /dev/null 2>&1; then echo "ok $*" else echo "FAILED $*" failed=1 fi } check R --version check quarto check check git config --global user.name check git config --global user.email check Rscript -e 'stopifnot(isTRUE(renv::status()$synchronized))' exit "$failed" ``` It omits `set -e` on purpose, so that one failure does not hide the others, and keeps `-u` and `pipefail`. `git config` with a key exits non-zero when the key is unset, which makes it a check rather than a listing. `Rscript -e 'renv::status()'` alone prints its report but exits zero even when it finds issues, so the last check tests the `synchronized` element of the result, which turns a report into an exit status. Run the script from a project directory so that the `renv` check has a lockfile to read; `PATH=/usr/bin:/bin bash check-machine.sh` makes the Quarto check fail. ::: ## Cheat sheet | Task | Command | |---|---| | Which R, which version | `R --version`; `which R` (`where R` on Windows) | | Manage R versions | `rig list`; `rig install 4.4.0`; `rig default 4.4.0` | | Check Quarto and its tools | `quarto check` | | Introduce yourself to Git | `git config --global user.name "..."`; `... user.email "..."` | | See Git settings | `git config --list` | | Where packages install | `.libPaths()[1]`; `find.package("pkg")` | | Turn off workspace restore | `usethis::use_blank_slate()` | | Start R clean | `R --vanilla` | | Read a secret | `Sys.getenv("NAME")`; `keyring::key_get("service")` | | Install WSL (admin PowerShell) | `wsl --install` | | Is my machine ready? | @tbl-workstation-ready | : The workstation at a glance. {#tbl-workstation-cheat-sheet} ## Further reading - [@bryan2019happygit], whose installation chapters cover Git, Git clients, and the R side of the setup in more detail. - The `rig` documentation at `github.com/r-lib/rig`. - Microsoft's 'Install WSL' guide at `learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/install`. ## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-04} 1. R stores installed packages in the directory returned by `.libPaths()[1]`, typically `~/Library/R/...` on macOS or `~/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/...` on Linux. With `renv` active in a project, the project's private library under `renv/library/` takes precedence, isolating the project's package versions from the user library and from other projects. 2. It supplies, from the previous session, every object the script uses but never creates, so the script runs in your session and fails (or runs on different objects) everywhere else. The script only appears to run from a clean start. Turn the restore off (`usethis::use_blank_slate()`) and test with `R --vanilla`. 3. `R --version`, `quarto check`, `git config --list`, and, inside a project that uses `renv`, `renv::status()`: the checklist in @tbl-workstation-ready.
